card.hook: Most people snap Rønne's streets and never find out what the town's story is. Bornholm Museum is the cheat sheet, and it makes a calm, honest photo that says exactly where you are.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon near Museumsparken, about 30 m south-west of the subject, and face north-east. That's far enough back to get the whole building in.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole building. If it won't fit, drop to 0.5x. Save zoom 2x for a doorway, a sign or a window.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the building up with them so the vertical lines stay straight, and leave a little space around the edges.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters a building like this, and it's often quieter then. An overcast day works too, because the colours look even.
card.selfie_here: Try the pavement in front of the museum on Sankt Mortens Gade, by the no. 29 entrance, which is the street frontage listed as its address. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the building over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: You can shoot the outside from public space, but entry and opening arrangements can change, so check the official site before you plan to go in.
card.challenge: Take your full-building shot, then find one small detail, like a door, a sign or a window, and zoom in for a second picture without stepping closer.
card.good_to_know: Bornholm Museum is the island's cultural history museum, and the story inside runs from the Palaeolithic to today. That includes Bronze Age and Iron Age finds and the years of occupation during the Second World War. The museum association dates back to 1893. It also looks after Erichsens Gård, the former Hjorths Fabrik terracotta factory and the citadel at Kastellet.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon near Museumsparken, about 30 m south-west of the subject, and face north-east. That's far enough back to get the whole building in.

selfie_spots.name: Sankt Mortens Gade, pavement in front of the museum at no. 29
selfie_spots.detail: on the pavement in front of the museum's facade, at the Sankt Mortens Gade 29 entrance
selfie_spots.why: No page describes a best selfie position, so this is only the street frontage named as the museum's address, which is the most likely place to get the building behind you.

selfie_research.notes: Weak result: none of the pages I found names a selfie spot or a passer-by photo position for Bornholms Museum, so the selfie spot above is a low-confidence fallback based only on the street address (Sankt Mortens Gade 29). A Wikimedia Commons photo of the museum lists its camera point at about 55.10238, 14.70343, roughly 10 m south of the museum's mapped point, but no street name is given for it, so I did not use it as a named spot. The selfie-stick rule I found (no selfie sticks in the cloakroom, no tripods) belongs to Bornholm Art Museum in Gudhjem, not this museum, so I did not include it. Checking the museum's own website or a local photo guide for Rønne would be the next step.

card.hook: Picture a small Danish street the way it looked long ago: a low roofline, a painted timber frame, and no showing off. That's Erichsens Gård, Rønne's best-preserved ordinary townsperson's house, and the plain look is exactly what makes it so nice to photograph.
card.stand_here: Head to the spot near Store Torvegade, about 95 m east of the subject, where the phone icon is on the map, and face west. From here you get the house in its street.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to show the house with its surroundings. Then try zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick the house out from a distance. Save zoom 0.5x for when you're right up against the walls.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and line the walls up with the vertical lines so the old house stands up straight.
card.best_time: Morning is a good choice, because the sun should be behind you when you face west. Overcast days work well too, since they suit the muted colours of the house.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera and stand with the house over your shoulder. Try zoom 0.5x if your phone has it, so more of the timber frame fits in behind you. Step back a little from the house to get the roofline in too.
card.rules_and_safety: Check the official Bornholm Museum site before you go to see if you can go inside.
card.challenge: Take three frames of the house at different distances: the whole street scene, the roof and timber frame, then a close-up of a door or window. Keep the walls straight in all three.
card.good_to_know: The house was built in 1806 and extended in the 1830s and 1840s. The architect Henning Pedersen lived here from 1816 to 1837, and the name comes from Thomas Erichsen, who bought it in 1838 and had 12 children with his wife. One of them, Vilhelmine, became the muse of the artists Kristian Zahrtmann and Holger Drachmann, and the house now belongs to the Bornholm Museum, which bought it in 1950.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to the spot near Store Torvegade, about 95 m east of the subject, where the phone icon is on the map, and face west. From here you get the house in its street.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a spot where visitors take a selfie with Erichsens Gård behind them, or a spot where a passer-by should photograph a visitor with the whole building. The searches returned only the museum's address and opening details (Laksegade 7, Rønne), Wikimedia photo records, general visitor listings, and a Rønne Byarkiv page. That archive page describes an old photo taken from the alley (smøgen) leading toward Erichsens gård, but it is a historical caption with the building in front of the camera, not a selfie or photo-spot recommendation, so I did not use it. The Rønne Byarkiv page also mentions a large elm tree beside Erichsens Gård on Laksegade, but no page recommends it as a photo position. No selfie-stick, tripod, or safety rule was stated on any page I found. The museum's own page says the garden is free to enter outside house opening hours (Monday to Thursday 10am-3pm in summer), which may matter for photos, but that is not a photo rule. Visitors could check the site on arrival, since one travel page only says non-flash photography is often permitted and advises checking guidelines on arrival. A further search on local photo guides or Laksegade street views may turn up named spots.

card.hook: You'd walk right past it if you didn't know better, because this yellow and brown timber-framed house looks like a cottage, not a theatre. That's the charm: warm colours, dark timber lines and a steep red roof.
card.stand_here: Stand near Østergade, about 50 m east of the theatre, at the phone icon on the map, and face west. The yellow and brown corner of Teaterstræde and Østergade should be right ahead of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural look. If the whole corner won't fit, drop to 0.5x but keep the building centred so the walls don't lean in. Zoom 2x or more, depending on your phone, is great for the timber pattern, windows and doors.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the yellow wall, then slide the brightness down a touch so the colours stay rich and the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Go in daytime, when the colours and timber lines show up clearly. A bright, overcast sky keeps the shadows soft. In the evening, switch on night mode and rest your phone against something solid to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Flip to the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and tuck the yellow and brown corner behind your shoulder. Hold the phone a little higher so the red roof sneaks into the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: You can photograph the outside from the street. If you want to see inside or catch a performance, check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Turn on the gridlines and line the corner of the building up with a vertical line, so the little theatre stands up straight with its roof on top and a strip of street underneath.
card.good_to_know: The building dates from 1783 and became a theatre in 1823. That makes it Denmark's oldest provincial theatre still in regular use, and it has been listed since 1938. It still stages plays, opera, cabaret and the annual Bornholmer Revue, and the Baroque-style auditorium inside holds 302 people.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near Østergade, about 50 m east of the theatre, at the phone icon on the map, and face west. The yellow and brown corner of Teaterstræde and Østergade should be right ahead of you.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a selfie spot or a photographer position for Rønne Theater, so I have not invented one. The only named places are the building's location at the western corner of Østergade and Teaterstræde (KultuNaut, https://www.kultunaut.dk/perl/sted/type-nynaut/nr-133271; Wikimedia Commons, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:R%C3%B8nne_Theater_-_1823.JPG) and the entrance from Østergade 7A (https://ronnetheater.dk/kontakt-og-adresse/). Those are location facts, not photo advice. Visitdenmark and bornholminfo describe the yellow half-timbered facade and say the building is in Teaterstræde, but they do not say where to stand. No selfie-stick or tripod rules were stated on any page I found. A local check on the ground would be needed before the app names a spot.

card.hook: Rønne's harbour has one landmark you can't miss: a church tower that pokes up above the town like it's checking on the boats. St. Nicolas' Church is a lovely jumble of old and newer parts, so it's a good subject for a quick phone snap.
card.stand_here: Stand near Kirkepladsen, about 10 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. The church fills the view in front of you, with the tower a little to one side.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x, because you're close and the building is tall. Switch to 1x for a calmer view of the walls, or 2x-5x to pick out the tower and roofline.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and line up the tower with a vertical line so it stays upright.
card.best_time: Around midday or early afternoon, when the south side you're facing is likely to be well lit. Early morning or evening gives softer, warmer light, but the front may then be in shade.
card.selfie_here: Head into the churchyard and try the short paths and viewpoints there, facing out over the harbour so the church sits behind you. Use the front camera, and zoom 0.5x if you want more of the church and tower over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the harbour quayside and aim up the slope at the church, while you stand in front of it so the whole church and tower are behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: It's a working parish church, so check the official site before you go for visiting times and any rules about going inside. Access can vary on Sundays and during services.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole church, then one close shot where the tower stands perfectly straight on a gridline. Which one wins?
card.good_to_know: A much smaller church, Knuds Kirke, stood here from about 1275, and you can still see some of its foundations at the north-east corner. The church was extended westwards around 1350, and the tower was added in 1550 and rebuilt in 1699. Inside, the altar was carved by Christian Kofoed in 1918, and the painting above it, showing Jesus calming the storm, is by Sven Havsteen Mikkelsen.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near Kirkepladsen, about 10 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. The church fills the view in front of you, with the tower a little to one side.

selfie_spots.name: Churchyard (kirkegården) viewpoints around St Nicolai Kirke, Kirkepladsen 20
selfie_spots.detail: on the short paths and viewpoints inside the churchyard, facing out over the harbour so the church sits behind you
selfie_spots.why: A travel guide describes the churchyard as offering harbour vistas and tower views over Rønne's red rooftops, which suits a photo with the church behind the visitor.

ask_someone_spot.name: Rønne harbour quayside, facing up toward Sankt Nicolai Kirke
ask_someone_spot.detail: stand on the harbour side and aim up the slope at the church, so the visitor stands in front with the whole church and tower behind them

sources.title: Rønne on Bornholm - Old Town, Harbour & Attractions (bornholm.de)

selfie_research.notes: The selfie spot is inferred: the guide places the churchyard viewpoints over the harbour and mentions tower photos, but no page names a specific selfie position with the church behind the visitor. The passer-by spot is a general harbour view toward the church, not a precise quay point. Access to the churchyard and church may vary on Sundays and during services, per the Evendo guide. No page I found states selfie stick or tripod rules. The given coordinates (55.09901, 14.69764) are within a few metres of the church coordinates on the sources (about 55.0988, 14.6974).

card.hook: Most lighthouses get a windy cliff all to themselves. This one is squeezed in between ordinary town houses, like it's squeezing onto a crowded bus. That's what makes it fun to photograph.
card.stand_here: Stand on Havnebakken, the street the tower stands on, and face north-east. From here the lighthouse is to the north-east, rising above the street and the houses on the slope, with the harbour basin below.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the tower, the street and the houses in one frame. Then try zoom 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) for a tighter shot of the lantern and the gallery. Only use 0.5x if you want lots of street, and keep your phone level so the tower doesn't look tilted.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line so it stands straight, with a bit of street and rooftops at the bottom to show how tall it is.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is kind to white paint and shows off the cast-iron detail. Early in the day the street is also likely to be quieter.
card.selfie_here: Try the benches beside the lighthouse on the short climb up the hill above the harbour. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold the phone a bit low and out so the tower is over your shoulder. We couldn't confirm which way the tower faces from the benches, so check the angle when you get there.
card.rules_and_safety: The tower isn't open inside, so this is a photo-from-outside stop.
card.challenge: Can you get the green lantern dome and the harbour basin in the same picture, with the tower standing perfectly straight on a grid line?
card.good_to_know: Locals call it Rønne Bagfyr. It was built in 1880 by the Bornholm firm H. Wichmann & Co, and it's cast iron with an eight-sided tapering body, 18 metres tall in all. It was restored and repainted in 2000, and it was taken out of service as a lighthouse in the late 1980s.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Havnebakken, the street the tower stands on, and face north-east. From here the lighthouse is to the north-east, rising above the street and the houses on the slope, with the harbour basin below.

selfie_spots.name: Benches by the lighthouse on Havnebakken hill
selfie_spots.detail: on the benches beside the lighthouse, on the short climb to the hill above the harbour
selfie_spots.why: A Visit Bornholm walking-tour page places benches beside the lighthouse on the hill above the harbour, with a panoramic view over the waterfront and rooftops, but it does not say which direction the tower faces from there.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found describes a best selfie angle with the Rønne Lighthouse behind the visitor, or a specific standing spot for a passer-by to frame the whole tower. The selfie spot above is the only lighthouse-area stop named, and it is inferred from a walking-tour page, so check the angle on arrival. Do not confuse this tower with Rønne Kongen, a separate granite light on the old pier that a Visit Bornholm page describes as a photo point; it is not the landmark you asked about. Sources disagree on height: one bornholm.de page gives 12 m (about 18 m with base), while Wikidata lists 18 m. The tower is not open inside, and no page gives selfie-stick or tripod rules or a safety point.
